body.text: A non-refundable investment tax credit (ITC) under Canada's SR&ED program reduces federal Part I tax payable but is not paid out in cash. Foreign-controlled and non-eligible public corporations earn non-refundable 15% ITCs, and unused non-refundable ITCs can be carried back 3 taxation years or carried forward 20 years under the Income Tax Act.

This report provides a legal, technical, and financial audit of Canada's research and development (R&D) tax incentives, subnational tax credits and patent boxes, direct innovation grants, compliance procedures, and judicial precedents as of November 15, 2026.

Canada's flagship R&D tax incentive—the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program under sections 37, 127, and 127.1 of the Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.))—underwent its largest legislative expansion in more than a decade when Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1) received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Enacting reforms first proposed in the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement and expanded in Federal Budget 2025 (Canada Strong, tabled November 4, 2025), Bill C-15 retroactively doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (yielding up to $2,100,000 per year in cash-refundable federal credits), widened the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extended the enhanced 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a three-year average gross revenue phase-out ($15 million–$75 million, into which Canadian-controlled private corporations [CCPCs] may also elect), and restored eligibility for depreciable SR&ED capital property, shared-use equipment (SUE), and qualifying equipment lease expenditures acquired or incurred after December 15, 2024. Operationally, on April 1, 2026, the CRA launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval process for Canadian businesses with under $25 million in annual gross business income, providing upfront technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks and cutting post-filing expenditure review service standards from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days for claims composed exclusively of pre-approved projects.

Most recently, Federal Budget 2026 (tabled November 5, 2026) proposed a major downstream expansion of SR&ED—subject to legislative enactment—to cover regulatory approval and certification testing as well as intellectual property (IP) registration and maintenance costs directly tied to an eligible SR&ED project for taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026 (January 1, 2027 for calendar-year corporations), alongside a proposed permanent Productivity Mega Deduction for qualifying capital assets acquired on or after September 15, 2026, while leaving a federal patent box unimplemented. At the subnational level, nine provinces and Yukon layer R&D tax credits onto federal SR&ED (reducing federal qualified expenditures as government assistance under subsection 127(18)), highlighted by Quebec's consolidated refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) (30% on the first $1,000,000 above the exclusion threshold and 20% thereafter for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025) and 2.0% Incentive Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (IDCI) patent box, Ontario's automatic restoration of post-December 15, 2024 capital property for its 8% refundable OITC (which retains its $3,000,000 cap) and 3.5% ORDTC, British Columbia's 2026 budget measure making its 10% SR&ED credit permanent, Alberta's refundable Innovation Employment Grant (8% base / 20% incremental up to $4,000,000, excluding post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures), and Saskatchewan's 10% R&D credit and 6.0% Commercial Innovation Incentive (SCII) patent box operating through June 30, 2027.
1. Statutory Architecture and Legislative Evolution Through November 2026
1.1 Core Provisions of the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations

Canada's federal R&D tax incentive system is codified within the federal Income Tax Act (ITA), R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), and Part XXIX (section 2900) of the Income Tax Regulations (ITR), C.R.C., c. 945. Unlike discretionary government grant programs that depend on annual departmental budget envelopes, SR&ED is a statutory entitlement accessible to any corporation, individual carrying on a sole proprietorship, partner of a partnership, or beneficiary of a trust carrying on business in Canada and incurring qualifying expenditures for SR&ED carried on in Canada.

The statutory design delivers support through two distinct but synchronized mechanisms: first, an immediate 100% deduction against business income (or an indefinite carryforward expenditure pool) under section 37; and second, a volume-based Investment Tax Credit (ITC) calculated on qualified SR&ED expenditures under sections 127 and 127.1.

body.text: 1.2 Enacted Reforms Under Bill C-15 (Royal Assent March 26, 2026)

Following two rounds of Department of Finance Canada public consultations initiated in 2024 on modernizing federal R&D support, the federal government unveiled an initial SR&ED reform blueprint in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement released on December 16, 2024. That statement initially proposed raising the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3,000,000 to $4,500,000, widening the prior-year taxable capital phase-out corridor from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extending the 35% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and restoring the pre-2014 eligibility of capital expenditures and equipment lease costs. Technical draft legislative amendments and explanatory notes were subsequently released by the Department of Finance in August 2025.

In Federal Budget 2025 (Canada Strong), tabled on November 4, 2025 by the Honourable François-Philippe Champagne, Minister of Finance and National Revenue, the government expanded the package by raising the proposed annual enhanced SR&ED expenditure limit from $4,500,000 directly to $6,000,000—effectively doubling the historical $3,000,000 ceiling—while confirming all other 2024 Fall Economic Statement enhancements and introducing CRA administrative reforms anchored by an elective Pre-Claim Approval mechanism effective April 1, 2026.

Every element of this statutory package became law when Bill C-15, the Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1, received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. For financial statement tax provision purposes under both IFRS and U.S. GAAP, the measures became enacted on March 26, 2026. However, for corporate tax compliance and retroactive T2 / T661 amendments, the statutory effective dates reach back to December 2024 along two distinct timelines. First, the entity and limit enhancements—specifically the $6,000,000 annual expenditure limit, the $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds, the extension of the 35% enhanced refundable ITC to ECPCs, and the CCPC election to apply the three-year average gross revenue phase-out structure—apply to taxation years that begin after December 15, 2024 (meaning on or after December 16, 2024, or beginning with the 2025 taxation year for calendar-year corporations). Second, the capital and lease restorations apply on a transaction-date basis: depreciable SR&ED capital property and shared-use equipment qualify if acquired (and available for use) after December 15, 2024, and SR&ED equipment lease costs qualify to the extent lease amounts first become payable (incurred) after December 15, 2024. Where a claimant's taxation year straddled December 15, 2024 (having begun before December 16, 2024), SR&ED operating-time percentages for leased or acquired equipment are measured across total operating time after December 15, 2024, whereas any depreciable property acquired between January 1, 2014 and December 15, 2024 remains permanently excluded.
1.3 Proposed Federal Budget 2026 Measures (Tabled November 5, 2026)

On November 5, 2026, Minister of Finance François-Philippe Champagne tabled Federal Budget 2026, introducing further proposed tax reforms affecting innovative enterprises that remain subject to parliamentary enactment as of November 15, 2026.

The centrepiece innovation proposal in Budget 2026 (pp. 117 and 402–403) widens the SR&ED program downstream to cover two categories of commercialization expenditures, provided they are directly linked to an underlying R&D project that qualifies under the existing SR&ED definition. Historically, SR&ED eligibility ceased the moment technological uncertainty was resolved, disqualifying regulatory trials, certification runs, and patenting fees. Under Budget 2026, qualifying SR&ED expenditures—earning the unchanged 35% enhanced rate (within the $6,000,000 expenditure limit) or 15% basic rate—would expand to encompass: (1) regulatory and certification testing, specifically tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to satisfy regulatory requirements for obtaining the first approval or certification of a new or improved product or process; and (2) intellectual property protection costs, specifically expenditures to register and maintain formal IP protection—covering patents, certificates of supplementary protection (CSPs), plant breeders' rights, and copyrighted software, whether registered in Canada or internationally—for IP developed in the course of an eligible SR&ED project. If IP whose registration or maintenance costs earned SR&ED tax support is later sold, recapture rules would recover the tax benefit. The Department of Finance projects this measure will deliver $930 million in support over five years and $235 million annually ongoing, and the CRA plans to publish sector-specific commercialization guidance. While one preliminary legal bulletin referenced expenses incurred on or after Budget Day, detailed tax advisory analyses citing Budget 2026's legislative annex (pp. 402–403) confirm the expansion is proposed to apply to taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026 (making January 1, 2027 the earliest applicable year for calendar-year corporations), with general marketing and unrelated commercial expenses remaining ineligible.

Equally significant for corporate IP structuring is what Ottawa omitted: despite holding consultations on a federal patent box regime in 2024 and referencing reduced IP commercialization tax rates in the December 2024 Fall Economic Statement and 2025 election platform, neither Budget 2025 nor Budget 2026 introduced a federal patent box. Tax practitioners note that folding IP protection and regulatory certification directly into SR&ED signals a federal preference for upfront R&D and commercialization cost offsets rather than preferential back-end income tax rates. Consequently, patent box incentives in Canada operate solely at the provincial level in Quebec (IDCI) and Saskatchewan (SCII).

Alongside SR&ED, Budget 2026 confirmed the proposed Productivity Mega Deduction (following draft legislative proposals released on September 15, 2026), a proposed permanent immediate 100% write-off for a broad range of capital assets acquired on or after September 15, 2026. Government and practitioner analyses estimate this measure will cover more than 65% of business investment (up from roughly 15%), cost $36 billion over five years, and lower Canada's marginal effective tax rate (METR) on new business investment from 13.0% to 6.4%—while excluding most long-lived buildings, goodwill, certain passenger vehicles, regulated natural gas distribution pipelines, and resource-depletion property, and requiring close review of enacting legislation regarding software, R&D assets, and patents. Finally, Budget 2026 proposed broader corporate and administrative simplifications, including a formal corporate loss transfer rule to replace complex loss-consolidation structures, an exemption for CCPCs from entity-level tax under the taxable preferred share regime for dividends paid after November 5, 2026, raising Form T1135 foreign property reporting thresholds from $100,000 to $200,000 (and simplified reporting from $250,000 to $500,000), a unified May 15 personal tax filing/payment date, and extended timeframes for individuals and graduated rate estates to file Notices of Objection (effective three months after enacting Royal Assent).
2. Scientific and Technological Eligibility Framework
2.1 Statutory Definition Under Subsection 248(1)

Canada's statutory definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) of the ITA aligns broadly with the OECD Frascati Manual while enforcing strict statutory boundaries interpreted by Canadian courts. Under subsection 248(1), "scientific research and experimental development" means systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis and that falls within one of four enumerated branches.

The first branch, paragraph (a) (Basic Research), encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view, occurring predominantly in university or fundamental research laboratories. The second branch, paragraph (b) (Applied Research), covers work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. The third and commercially dominant branch, paragraph (c) (Experimental Development), covers work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing (including incremental improvements), materials, devices, products, or processes. The fourth branch, paragraph (d) (Eligible Support Work), admits work with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, strictly to the extent that such work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.

Subsection 248(1) simultaneously carves out specific excluded activities that cannot qualify as SR&ED even when technically complex, including market research or sales promotion; quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; research in the social sciences or the humanities; prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; style changes; and routine data collection. Under current enacted law, downstream commercialization and IP protection fall outside SR&ED, subject to the pending Budget 2026 proposals for taxation years starting on or after November 5, 2026.
2.2 CRA Eligibility Guidelines: The "Why" and "How" Requirements

Over the past decade, the CRA retired legacy Information Circular IC 86-4R3 and subsequently replaced its Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy with the unified Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives. Emphasizing that the statutory definition in subsection 248(1) did not change, the CRA Guidelines consolidate the statutory text and judicial Five-Question Test into two mandatory requirements—the "Why" and the "How".

The "Why" requirement asks why the work was undertaken: the claimant must establish that at the onset of the work, a genuine scientific or technological uncertainty existed—meaning that whether a desired result or objective could be achieved, or how to achieve it, was not known or determinable on the basis of generally available scientific or technological knowledge or experience. Because overcoming such an obstacle requires pushing beyond known practice, the investigation must seek a scientific or technological advancement—the generation of new scientific or technological knowledge that advances understanding in the underlying field, rather than merely achieving commercial novelty, product uniqueness, aesthetic design iteration, feature expansion, or cost efficiency.

The "How" requirement asks how the investigation was prosecuted: the work must be conducted as a systematic investigation or search in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis performed by qualified individuals. This requires examining the baseline state of knowledge and its technical shortcomings at project inception, formulating explicit hypotheses aimed at resolving the uncertainty, designing and executing structured experiments or mathematical/computational analyses to test those hypotheses, recording measurable results in chronological order, and drawing logical technical conclusions that refine subsequent iterations.

Under CRA project-grouping policy (Group Work into SR&ED Projects and Guide T4088), an SR&ED project is defined at the level necessary to capture the set of interrelated activities—including commensurate paragraph 248(1)(d) support work—collectively required to attempt to achieve a defined scientific or technological advancement by overcoming specific technological uncertainties. Claimants must carve out this eligible slice from broader commercial product roadmaps. Under Guide T4088, project eligibility terminates on the date the claimant achieves the advancement by resolving the uncertainties, determines that the uncertainties cannot be resolved, or terminates the project for any reason.
2.3 Objective Competency Standard vs. Routine Engineering

In CRA technical reviews—particularly in software development and artificial intelligence, with software accounting for 42.6% of all SR&ED tax credits allowed according to CRA 2025–2026 statistics cited by industry analysts, as well as in manufacturing process engineering—the primary ground for audit denial is that claimed work represents routine engineering or standard practice.

Canadian tax law enforces an objective standard for technological uncertainty: whether a problem could be resolved through routine engineering or standard procedures is judged against the knowledge base accessible to competent professionals in the relevant field, never the subjective knowledge gaps of the taxpayer's internal staff. Simply adopting off-the-shelf AI models, integrating commercial APIs, writing complex business logic, or debugging software without underlying algorithmic, architectural, or hardware-constraint uncertainty does not qualify; conversely, formulating and testing novel model architectures, sensor-fusion pipelines, or compression techniques where published methods fail to meet hard latency or accuracy limits can qualify. Similarly, system uncertainty arises where integrating known technologies imposes conflicting physical, chemical, or computational constraints whose combined behaviour cannot be predicted by competent specialists using established design methods. Crucially, failing to achieve a technical or commercial objective does not disqualify an SR&ED claim: proving through systematic experimentation why a hypothesized solution fails under given constraints generates valid technological advancement.
3. Federal Tax Credit Rates, Expenditure Limits, Phase-Outs, and Refundability
3.1 Dual-Incentive Mechanics: Section 37 Deduction Pool and Section 127 ITCs

Eligible SR&ED spending generates two cumulative federal benefits that interact across consecutive taxation years. First, allowable current SR&ED expenditures (s. 37(1)(a)) and restored post-December 15, 2024 ASA capital expenditures (s. 37(1)(b))—reduced by government and non-government assistance (s. 37(1)(d)) and any provincial super-allowance benefits (s. 37(1)(d.1))—enter the section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures. Taxpayers may deduct up to 100% of a positive pool balance in computing business income for the current taxation year or carry unused balances forward indefinitely to shelter future taxable income taxed at higher marginal corporate rates. However, if the corporation undergoes a loss restriction event (an acquisition of control), subsection 37(6.1) and paragraph 37(1)(h) restrict carryforward of the pre-acquisition SR&ED pool to income from the same or a similar business.

Second, qualified SR&ED expenditures earn federal Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) under subsection 127(5) and 127(10.1) at either the 35% enhanced rate or 15% basic rate. Unused non-refundable ITCs may be carried back 3 preceding taxation years (capped at the lesser of the current year's unneeded ITC and the prior year's Part I tax otherwise payable in excess of that prior year's available ITC) and carried forward 20 subsequent taxation years. Acquisition-of-control rules similarly block pre-acquisition ITCs from being carried forward to post-acquisition years and block post-acquisition ITCs from being carried back to pre-acquisition years. Under subsection 127.1(3), any SR&ED ITC refunded in cash is deemed to have been deducted against Part I tax payable, reducing carryover pools dollar for dollar. Crucially, federal SR&ED ITCs are taxable in the subsequent taxation year: any federal ITC deducted against Part I tax or refunded in Year 1 reduces the section 37 expenditure pool in Year 2, and if that reduction drives the pool negative (or applies to the Prescribed Proxy Amount), the excess is included directly in Year 2 taxable income under paragraphs 12(1)(t) and 12(1)(v) (or reduces undepreciated capital cost [UCC] in the following year for Shared-Use Equipment).

body.text: Several critical structural distinctions govern this enacted rate table. First, a qualifying CCPC, an "other CCPC" under subsection 127.1(2.01), or an ECPC with the full $6,000,000 expenditure limit and $6,000,000 of qualified current expenditures (including PPA) earns up to 35% × $6,000,000 = $2,100,000 per year in 100% cash-refundable federal ITCs—doubling the pre-December 16, 2024 maximum of $1,050,000. Second, for restored capital expenditures within the $6,000,000 expenditure limit, the 35% enhanced ITC is 40% refundable in cash (yielding an immediate 35% × 40% = 14.0% cash refund on eligible capital cost, while the remaining 21.0% ITC offsets Part I tax payable or carries back 3 / forward 20 years).

Third, to qualify as an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) throughout a taxation year (subsection 127(10.1)), a corporation must be resident in Canada, have a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange (or have elected, or been designated by the Minister of National Revenue, to be a public corporation), and not be controlled directly or indirectly in any manner whatever by non-resident persons; Canadian-resident corporations of which all or substantially all (≥90%) of the shares are owned by one or more ECPCs also qualify. However, unlike a "Qualifying Corporation" CCPC—which continues to earn a 40% cash refund on the 15% basic ITC above its $6,000,000 expenditure limit—an ECPC receives zero cash refund on expenditures exceeding its expenditure limit. Fourth, prior-year taxable income does not grind down a CCPC's $6,000,000 enhanced expenditure limit; instead, exceeding the subsection 127.1(2) and (4) "qualifying income limit" simply shifts a CCPC from "Qualifying Corporation" status to "Other CCPC" status under subsection 127.1(2.01), preserving 100% refundability on the 35% current credit up to its expenditure limit while eliminating the 40% refund on the 15% basic credit over the limit. Finally, partnerships never qualify for the 35% enhanced rate; partnership SR&ED expenditures flow through to partners at the 15% basic rate, with CRA's published table listing a 40% refund rate subject to specific partner-level limitations (such as non-refundability for non-qualifying corporate partners).
3.3 Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Formulas and Group Allocation Rules
For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the $6,000,000 baseline expenditure limit phases out on a straight-line basis between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000 under two statutory methods.

Under the Taxable Capital Method (Default for CCPCs, ITA s. 127(10.2)), the $6,000,000 expenditure limit begins to shrink once the combined taxable capital employed in Canada (determined under Part I.3 principles) in the immediately preceding taxation year of the CCPC and all associated CCPCs reaches $15,000,000, decreasing by $1 for every $10 of prior-year taxable capital over $15,000,000 until becoming nil ($0) at $75,000,000. Practitioners must note that this $15 million–$75 million SR&ED phase-out corridor is wider than the federal Small Business Deduction (SBD) taxable capital grind, which still eliminates the $500,000 federal SBD limit between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital.

Under the Three-Year Average Gross Revenue Method (Mandatory for ECPCs; Elective for CCPCs, ITA ss. 127(10.31), 127(10.32) & 127(10.6)), the $6,000,000 limit is reduced on the same straight-line 1-for-10 slope when average annual gross revenue over the preceding three fiscal years (as reported in financial statements) exceeds $15,000,000, reaching nil ($0) at $75,000,000. For ECPCs that belong to a consolidated group, the $6,000,000 limit is shared across the group and computed from the annual revenue reported in the group's consolidated financial statements. Crucially, Bill C-15 allows CCPCs to elect into this three-year average gross revenue formula in place of the taxable capital test—a major planning lever for venture-backed biotechnology, cleantech, semiconductor, and hardware CCPCs whose large equity or convertible-debt rounds push taxable capital past $15 million (or even past $75 million) while revenues remain below $15 million. Where a CCPC is associated with other CCPCs, all associated CCPCs in the group must jointly elect to use the revenue method on a prescribed form, summing the three-year average financial-statement revenue of every current group member regardless of whether those corporations were associated throughout the entire three-year lookback.

Associated CCPCs must allocate their single shared expenditure limit using Schedule T2SCH49 (updated in May and October 2026), while consolidated ECPCs and revenue-electing CCPCs must file the prescribed revenue allocation agreement. Under CRA policy, if an associated or consolidated group fails to file the required allocation agreement within 30 days of a CRA request, the CRA will determine the expenditure limit for the group to be nil ($0). If a corporation has a short taxation year of fewer than 365 days, its allocated expenditure limit is prorated by the ratio of days in the short taxation year to 365 (for example, $6,000,000 × 273 ÷ 365 = $4,487,671), and subsection 127(10.5) imposes anti-duplication proration where a corporation has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year while associated with another group member.
4. Qualifying Expenditures, Overhead Elections, Capital Restoration, and Recapture
4.1 Salaries, Wages, Specified Employees, and Foreign R&D Limits

Salaries and wages typically constitute the largest component of a Canadian SR&ED claim and simultaneously govern the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount. Under ITA s. 248(1), s. 37(8), and the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, claimable remuneration is bounded by strict functional, timing, and shareholder-employee rules.

Under the Proxy Method, only T4 gross salaries and wages paid to or incurred for employees for the proportion of time spent directly engaged ("hands-on" experimentation, technical analysis, non-executive direct technical supervision, and commensurate paragraph 248(1)(d) support work) in SR&ED in Canada can be claimed on the salary lines; clerical, purchasing, accounting, and human-resources staff cannot be claimed separately because their cost is captured inside the 55% PPA. Under the Traditional Method, hands-on, direct supervisory, and direct support salaries are claimed on the direct wage lines, while administrative salaries directly related and incremental to SR&ED may be claimed as overhead on Line 360. Across both direct wage calculations, SR&ED salaries and wages exclude the employer's share of payroll-related benefits (CPP, EI, provincial health taxes, workers' compensation, and group insurance—though incremental benefits may enter Line 360 under Traditional overhead), stock option benefits, retiring allowances, and extended vacation or sick leave (with CRA administrative practice permitting reasonable actual-cost estimates excluding GST/HST/PST for certain automobile taxable benefits, and treating regular payroll amounts meeting strict procedures accordingly). Furthermore, any accrued salary, wage, or remuneration not actually paid within 180 days after tax year-end is completely excluded from both the section 37 deduction pool and qualified expenditures for ITCs.

Heightened statutory caps apply to specified employees—defined as any employee who does not deal at arm's length with the employer (such as a spouse, sibling, or controlling individual) or who is a "specified shareholder" owning, directly or together with non-arm's length persons, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation. First, under subsection 37(9), all bonuses and remuneration based on profits paid to a specified employee are 100% disallowed. Second, under subsections 37(9.1)–(9.5), a specified employee's maximum allowable SR&ED salary is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by days employed over 365 and shared across associated corporations via Form T1174. Third, when calculating the 55% PPA salary base under ITR Regulation 2900(7) and (8), bonuses, profit-based pay, and taxable benefits are excluded for every employee (Reg. 2900(9)), and each specified employee's PPA salary base inclusion is further capped at the lesser of: (a) 75% of the specified employee's total eligible salary/wages (which bites even if an owner-manager spent 100% of the year on hands-on R&D—for example, a founder paid $200,000 adds at most $150,000 to the PPA base), and (b) 2.5 × YMPE × (days employed ÷ 365), with a single 2.5 × YMPE ceiling shared across associated corporations.

body.text: Although work performed outside Canada generally earns zero SR&ED tax credits, subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) provide a narrow exception for permissible salary or wages of employees carrying on SR&ED outside Canada (flagged at Form T661 Line 265): such wages enter both the section 37(1) pool and the federal ITC base up to a maximum of 10% of total salaries and wages for SR&ED carried on in Canada during the year, provided the foreign work is directly undertaken by the taxpayer's employees (never foreign subcontractors), relates to a business of the taxpayer, and is solely in support of SR&ED carried on in Canada by the taxpayer. Any foreign R&D current expenditures outside that 10% employee cap may only be deducted against current-year income under subsection 37(2), earning no section 37 pool carryforward and no ITC.
4.2 Subcontractors, Third-Party Payments, Non-Arm's Length Rules, and Materials

Payments to arm's-length Canadian subcontractors performing basic research, applied research, experimental development, or eligible paragraph 248(1)(d) support work in Canada on the claimant's behalf are 100% deductible in the section 37 pool, but only 80% of the eligible contract expenditure enters qualified expenditures for ITC calculation (ITA s. 127(9)) to strip out the contractor's commercial profit markup. Two strict statutory disqualifications apply: first, any portion of a subcontract performed outside Canada earns $0 in ITCs; second, any SR&ED contract amount paid or payable to a person or partnership that is not a "taxable supplier" (such as a foreign vendor lacking a Canadian permanent establishment) is 100% excluded from qualified expenditures for ITC purposes. Contracts and invoices should segregate eligible Canadian SR&ED tasks and specify IP ownership. Third-party payments (reported on Form T1263) made to approved Canadian universities, colleges, research institutes, or non-profit SR&ED corporations for SR&ED in Canada that the claimant is entitled to exploit in its business likewise enter the section 37 pool at 100% and qualified ITC expenditures at 80%.

Where SR&ED is subcontracted to a non-arm's length party, the payer cannot claim the contract payment as a qualified expenditure (s. 37(14) look-through and Part 4 exclusions); instead, the non-arm's length performer either claims its own underlying SR&ED costs or transfers qualified expenditures (up to the contract price) to the related payer by filing Form T1146 under subsection 127(13). Purchases of goods or non-SR&ED services from non-arm's length suppliers are capped at the related supplier's actual cost under subsection 127(11.6) (adjusted on Form T661 Line 543). Additionally, under the 180-day unpaid non-wage rule (subsection 127(9)), current expenditures other than salaries or wages (such as subcontractor invoices, materials, or Traditional overheads) that remain unpaid 180 days after year-end stay in the section 37 deduction pool for Year 1, but must be subtracted on Line 528 so they earn zero ITC in Year 1; when subsequently paid, they enter qualified expenditures in the year of payment (at 80% for arm's-length contracts).

Costs of materials consumed (rendered virtually worthless or destroyed during testing) or materials transformed (incorporated into prototypes, custom builds, or experimental production runs) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada qualify at 100% for both the section 37 pool and federal ITCs, provided claimants retain purchase invoices and build-consumption logs (general studio or office supplies are excluded and subsumed within overhead). However, materials transformed into a prototype or commercial asset carry 20-year ITC recapture exposure if later sold or converted to commercial use.
4.3 Overhead Elections: Proxy Method (55% PPA) vs. Traditional Method

Under subsection 37(10), every claimant must elect on Form T661 between the Proxy Method (Line 160) and the Traditional Method (Line 162) for each taxation year; once filed, the election is legally irrevocable for that taxation year.

Because the Proxy Method requires zero overhead itemization, engineering-heavy teams almost always elect Proxy unless provable incremental Traditional overheads—such as dedicated cloud GPU training clusters in AI firms whose compute bills exceed 55% of direct salaries, or owner-operated firms whose PPA base is severely compressed by the 75% / 2.5 × YMPE specified employee cap—surpass the 55% PPA.
4.4 Restored Capital Property, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Equipment Leases

Pursuant to Bill C-15 and the CRA's updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026), and SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026), equipment and depreciable assets acquired or leased after December 15, 2024 qualify along discrete statutory pathways. Claimants must maintain contemporaneous equipment logbooks recording dates of use, project ties, operators, operating hours, and SR&ED versus commercial usage, and ensure financial accounting capitalizes depreciable SR&ED assets consistently rather than expensing them while claiming SR&ED capital treatment.

body.text: 4.5 Government Assistance Grinding and 20-Year ITC Recapture Rules

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18), both the section 37 deduction pool and qualified SR&ED expenditures must be reduced by any government assistance (including provincial/territorial R&D tax credits, grants, forgivable loans, and wage subsidies), non-government assistance, and SR&ED contract payments that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before its income tax filing-due date for the year. Excess assistance within a related group is allocated via Form T1145 (updated May 15, 2026 to separate current and capital assistance on Lines 015 and 020 and reported on Form T661 Lines 513, 518, and 540). Under CRA's Shared-Use-Equipment Policy, if government assistance received on an SUE asset exceeds its 25% First-Term SUE qualified expenditure, the unused assistance balance carries forward to reduce the 25% Second-Term SUE qualified expenditure in the following year. Subsequent repayments of assistance restore eligible expenditures at the ITC rate applicable when the assistance was originally received.

Conversely, under subsections 127(27)–(35) and the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, if a taxpayer earned an SR&ED ITC on purchased property—specifically materials transformed into a custom product, commercial asset, or experimental production unit, ASA capital equipment, or Shared-Use Equipment (SUE)—and within 20 preceding taxation years sells that property (or another product incorporating it) or converts it to commercial use, SR&ED ITC recapture applies. Recapture adds directly to Part I tax payable (computed on Schedule 31 or Form T2038(IND), while restoring a corresponding deduction to the section 37 pool under paragraph 37(1)(c.2)) an amount equal to the lesser of: (1) the SR&ED ITC originally earned on the property, and (2) the original ITC percentage applied to the proceeds of disposition (for arm's-length sales) or fair market value (for commercial conversions or non-arm's length transfers). For SUE, conversion to commercial use occurs only when SR&ED usage becomes incidental (all or substantially all commercial use), and only 25% (one term) or 50% (two terms) of proceeds or fair market value enters the recapture formula. Crucially, under subsection 127(32), SR&ED salaries, wages, and overhead (including PPA) are never subject to ITC recapture, because "cost of the particular property" is limited strictly to acquisition cost paid to a transferor. Under current enacted law, selling or licensing internally developed intellectual property also triggers no recapture where IP ownership accrued to the claimant as generated (whereas Budget 2026 proposes a targeted recapture rule if newly proposed IP registration/maintenance claims are later followed by an IP sale).
5. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credits and Subnational Patent Boxes
5.1 Complete Cross-Canada Jurisdictional Matrix (2025–2026)

Nine provinces and Yukon supplement federal SR&ED with subnational R&D tax credits; Prince Edward Island, Northwest Territories, and Nunavut have no R&D tax credit. Every jurisdiction's credit is administered by the CRA via the federal T2 return except Quebec (administered by Revenu Québec on the CO-17 return) and Alberta (administered by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration [TRA] on the AT1 return).

body.text: 5.2 Quebec: CRIC Reform, IDCI Patent Box, and C3i

Quebec administers Canada's most distinctive subnational innovation tax regime, comprehensively modernized for 2025–2026. For taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, Quebec abolished multiple legacy R&D tax credits and unified them into the fully refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC)—designated on Revenu Québec Form RD-1029.8.CR-T as the Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC) and filed within 12 months after the CO-17 corporate return deadline. While Quebec harmonizes its core R&D definition with federal law and relies on the CRA for scientific review of R&D work, CRIC broke new ground by extending provincial tax credits to pre-commercialization activities conducted in Quebec in conjunction with Quebec R&D—specifically: (1) regulatory tests, technological validations, and studies aimed at obtaining initial commercialization approval or certification, and (2) product design covering form, aesthetics, improved functionality, and material choice (supported by Form RD-1029.8.PR-T).

To earn CRIC, a corporation's qualified Quebec expenditures must first exceed an applicable exclusion threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 (prorated for short taxation years) or the sum of the Quebec personal income tax basic personal amount per involved employee adjusted for the proportion of time devoted to eligible R&D and pre-commercialization. Above that threshold, corporations earn a 30% refundable credit on up to $1,000,000 of net qualified expenditures (allocated among associated corporations on Form RD-1029.8.EN-T) and a 20% refundable credit on all excess spending (corporate members of a partnership earn the 20% base rate only, without access to the 30% enhanced tier). Qualified CRIC expenditures include 100% of eligible Quebec wages, 50% of amounts paid to Quebec subcontractors, 50% of payments to eligible public research centres, research consortia, or university entities, and 100% of never-previously-used depreciable equipment acquired and available for use almost exclusively in eligible Quebec activities (excluding land, buildings, and Large Investment Project tax-holiday assets). If CRIC-supported property ceases to be used solely in Quebec within 730 consecutive days from initial use, Revenu Québec recovers the credit via a special clawback tax.

On the commercialization side, Quebec's Incentive Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (IDCI — Form CO-737.18.CI)—which replaced the historical Deduction for Innovative Manufacturing Corporations (Form CO-737.SI) for taxation years beginning after December 31, 2020 (L.Q. 2021, c. 14, ss. 76, 198)—lowers Quebec's general 11.5% corporate tax rate by 9.5 percentage points to an effective 2.0% rate (an 82.6% [0.826] income deduction factor, yielding a 17.0% combined federal-Quebec corporate tax rate) on qualified income (embedded sales/leases, intrinsically related services, royalties, and infringement damages, excluding capital gains) from patents, CSPs, plant breeders' rights, and copyrighted software. OECD BEPS Action 5 nexus compliance is enforced via a cumulative 7-year moving-average Quebec R&D nexus fraction (current year plus six preceding years, excluding CRIC pre-commercialization expenses). Separately, Quebec's refundable Tax Credit for Investment and Innovation (C3i — Form CO-1029.8.36.II) provides 15% to 25% (per current practitioner guidance, elevated from initial 10%–20% baseline rates depending on economic vitality zone and acquisition period) on new manufacturing equipment (CCA Classes 29, 43, 53 above a $12,500 per-asset exclusion) and IT hardware / ERP software (Classes 50 and 12 above a $5,000 per-asset exclusion), while Quebec's small business tax rate dropped from 3.2% to 2.2% (11.2% combined with federal) for taxation years beginning after April 29, 2026 for CCPCs meeting Quebec's 5,500 paid-hours threshold.
5.3 Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, OBRITC, and Stacking Arithmetic

Under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), corporations with an Ontario permanent establishment stack up to three provincial R&D credits onto federal SR&ED. The Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — s. 96, Schedule 566) provides an 8% refundable credit on up to $3,000,000 of qualified Ontario expenditures ($240,000 maximum annual refund, shared across associated corporations and prorated for short years). Crucially, Ontario did not match Bill C-15's $6,000,000 expenditure limit or $15M–$75M phase-out: the OITC cap remains $3,000,000 (so spending between $3 million and $6 million earns the federal 35% credit but $0 in OITC) and phases out between $500,000 and $800,000 of prior-year taxable income and $25,000,000 and $50,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital. However, Ontario automatically paralleled Bill C-15's restoration of 100% of SR&ED capital expenditures for depreciable property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, as confirmed in Ontario's 2026 Fall Economic Statement annex (overriding unupdated legacy text on ontario.ca that as of late October 2026 still cited the post-2013 capital exclusion).

Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Schedule 508) provides a 3.5% non-refundable credit on qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures (reduced by OITC claimed, with no upper expenditure limit, 3-year carryback / 20-year carryforward, and restored post-December 15, 2024 capital eligibility subject to Ontario recapture rules). Because an unutilized ORDTC added to carryforwards is "reasonably expected to be received," it grinds down the current-year 35% cash-refundable federal ITC base under ITA s. 127(18) unless the claimant formally waives/renounces the ORDTC on or before its filing-due date (OITC may also be waived under s. 96(14)). Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Schedules 568 & 569) provides a 20% refundable credit on up to $20,000,000 ($4,000,000 max credit) of eligible contract payments to qualifying Ontario universities, colleges, and hospital research institutes.

body.text: In Scenario B, if the CCPC is loss-making and waives the $49,910 non-refundable ORDTC on or before its filing-due date, its federal 35% cash refund rises by 35% × $49,910 = $17,469 (to $499,100), lifting immediate cash recovery from $605,632 to $623,100. Claimants must also account for Schedule 1 income inclusions: the portion of a provincial credit attributable to the 55% PPA enters taxable income in the year received, while federal ITCs are taxed in the following year under s. 12(1)(t).
5.4 Western, Prairie, Atlantic, and Territorial Regimes

In British Columbia, sections 97–103 of the Income Tax Act (British Columbia) (Form T666, due 18 months after year-end) provide a 10% refundable credit for CCPCs up to their expenditure limit ($300,000 max cash refund) and a 10% non-refundable credit on excess spending and for non-CCPCs (3-year carryback / 10-year carryforward, with optional renunciation of non-refundable credits); BC Budget 2026 made the BC SR&ED credit permanent.

In Alberta, the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) (Alberta Corporate Tax Act, ss. 26.95–26.99, claimed on AT1 Schedule 29 [AS29]) pays a 100% refundable credit on up to $4,000,000 of annual Alberta R&D expenditures (phased out between $10 million and $50 million of taxable capital): 8% on eligible spending up to the corporation's base spending level (the average qualifying Alberta R&D spend over the two preceding taxation years), and 20% on spending exceeding that two-year base (mathematically equivalent to an 8% base credit on all eligible spend up to $4M plus a 12% incremental enhancement on spending above the two-year average—never 28%). Two 2026 compliance rules are vital: first, Alberta Schedule 29 (AS29) explicitly excludes capital expenditures made after December 15, 2024; second, while some practitioner summaries cite a 15-month post-year-end deadline, the CRA's official provincial guide specifies the IEG filing deadline as 15 months after the corporation's filing due date.

In Saskatchewan, alongside a 10% R&D credit (refundable for CCPCs on an initial tier—cited in secondary guides variously as $100,000 max credit or first $2M spend with a $1M cap—and non-refundable with 3-year carryback / 10-year carryforward otherwise), the province operates the Saskatchewan Commercial Innovation Incentive (SCII) patent box. Evaluated technically in partnership with NRC IRAP, SCII lowers Saskatchewan's general corporate tax rate from 12% to 6.0% for 10 consecutive years—extended to 15 years where at least 50% of related R&D occurred in Saskatchewan—for a single-purpose corporation commercializing qualifying patents, trade secrets, or copyrights (including "cascading" incremental and "forking" major derivative goods or processes) that have no Canadian market equivalent or represent an exceptional advance. Certificate holders can defer the start of their benefit window or refile up to 3 prior years and can stack SCII with SR&ED and IRAP; continuous intake runs until June 30, 2027. Manitoba provides a 15% R&D credit (50% refundable [7.5% cash] for in-house R&D; 100% refundable [15% cash] under eligible Manitoba research institute contracts; 3-year carryback / 20-year carryforward, with secondary guides noting a 12-month post-year-end filing deadline). New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Yukon also provide CRA-administered refundable R&D credits, whereas PEI, Northwest Territories, and Nunavut have no R&D credit. Notice also that software and digital studios across Ontario (OIDMTC, up to 40%), BC (IDMTC, 17.5%), Quebec (Multimedia Titles, up to 37.5%), and Nova Scotia (Digital Media, 50%) can evaluate interactive digital media credits alongside SR&ED where non-duplication rules permit.
6. Direct Federal Innovation Grants and Stacking Coordination
6.1 Core Non-Dilutive Federal Innovation Programs in 2026

Significant institutional restructuring reshaped Canada's direct federal R&D funding landscape across 2025 and 2026. The National Research Council of Canada's Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) remains the anchor non-repayable grant program for incorporated Canadian SMEs, reimbursing up to 80% of internal R&D technical labour (plus eligible Canadian contractor costs) via milestone payments during project execution ($75,000 median grant). Following the wind-down of standalone intakes at Sustainable Development Technology Canada (SDTC), federal clean-technology R&D funding was folded into NRC IRAP Clean Technology, which received $298 million in renewed funding in Federal Budget 2026. In addition, Budget 2025 committed $75 million over three years (starting 2026–27) to NRC to extend IP Assist, funding IP strategy and patenting support for IRAP firms.

For large industrial, clean-economy, and advanced manufacturing capital projects, Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) transitioned the former Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) into the Strategic Response Fund (SRF)—requiring mandatory pre-consultation and a $10 million minimum contribution ($20 million+ project scale), structured primarily as repayable contributions and reinforced by $1 billion in additional funding from 2028–29 in Budget 2026. Meanwhile, the Canada Digital Adoption Program (CDAP) closed in 2025 with no federal replacement, and Innovative Solutions Canada (ISC) saw its annual R&D procurement budget reduced by $70 million per year starting in 2025–26. Conversely, AI, compute, and dual-use defence R&D expanded through $925.6 million in federal AI/cloud infrastructure funding, Canada's AI for All national strategy launched June 4, 2026, Global Innovation Clusters ($1M–$5M consortium matching projects, though Scale AI's training stream paused intakes in 2026), $68.2 million over three years in Budget 2025 across the Department of National Defence (DND), ISED, NRC, and Communications Security Establishment (CSE), and Budget 2026's Defence Drone Initiative.
6.2 Grant-to-SR&ED Stacking Mechanics

Direct R&D contributions such as NRC IRAP stack cleanly with SR&ED on the exact same project when ITA s. 127(18) assistance rules and ITR Regulation 2900(4) proxy rules are modelled together. Specifically, while an IRAP grant received or receivable by the filing-due date reduces the section 37 pool and qualified SR&ED expenditures dollar for dollar, the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount is calculated on the gross eligible SR&ED salary base BEFORE subtracting the IRAP wage grant. For example, if a qualifying CCPC pays a developer $100,000 for 100% SR&ED work and receives an 80% NRC IRAP wage reimbursement ($80,000), the 55% PPA still generates $55,000 of notional overhead on the full $100,000 salary, leaving $100,000 wages + $55,000 PPA − $80,000 IRAP assistance = $75,000 of net federal qualified SR&ED expenditures—generating an additional $75,000 × 35% = $26,250 in refundable federal SR&ED cash on top of the $80,000 IRAP grant ($106,250 combined gross cash recovery on $100,000 of payroll, prior to provincial R&D credits and next-year s. 12(1)(t) tax).
7. Governance, Filing Compliance, Form T661 Architecture, and Pre-Claim Approval
7.1 Institutional Roles, Prescribed Forms, and Statutory Deadlines

The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) administers SR&ED through specialized Coordinating Tax Services Offices (CTSOs), pairing Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) with Financial Reviewers (FRs). Between May 15 and May 29, 2026, the CRA published a modernized suite of prescribed forms (and Guide T4088-26e) implementing Bill C-15.

Corporate claimants must file Form T661 (Version 26, released May 15, 2026) together with Schedule T2SCH31 (individuals and trusts file Form T2038(IND)), supported where applicable by Schedule T2SCH49 (associated CCPC expenditure limit allocation), Form T1174 (associated specified employee salary allocation), Form T1145 (non-arm's length assistance allocation), Form T1146 (non-arm's length contract expenditure transfer), and Form T1263 (third-party payments). Filing on an outdated version of Form T661 can delay claim processing.
Version 26 of Form T661 incorporates critical structural updates across its parts:

items: Part 1 & Part 2 (Technical Narratives & CRDC Codes): Adds fields for Canadian Research and Development Classification (CRDC) codes and Pre-Claim Approval case numbers. Claimants with more than 20 projects may submit Part 2 for the 20 largest projects in dollar value at filing while retaining the rest on file. Section B enforces hard word ceilings that must be written in clear, factual technical prose by (or directly with) the engineers/scientists who performed the work: Line 242 (Scientific or technological uncertainties — max 350 words), Line 244 (Work performed in the tax year to overcome those uncertainties — max 700 words), and Line 246 (Scientific or technological advancements achieved or attempted — max 350 words).

Parts 3, 4, 5 & 6 (Dual-Column Current/Capital Schedules): Captures the irrevocable Proxy (Line 160) vs. Traditional (Line 162) election, restored equipment leases (Lines 350 and 355), Traditional overhead (Line 360), and restored ASA capital property (Line 390). Current and capital amounts flow in separate columns through Part 4—adding PPA (Line 502) and SUE (Line 504) and deducting assistance (Lines 513, 518, 540), 180-day unpaid non-wage costs (Line 528), used-equipment/prescribed exclusions (Line 532), non-taxable supplier contracts, and non-arm's length adjustments (Lines 543–546) to arrive at Line 559 / Line 570 qualified expenditures. Part 6 splits into Part 6A (project costs including Box 759 for post-December 15, 2024 equipment leases), Part 6B (ASA capital expenditures), and Part 6C (20 most expensive SUE properties).

Part 9 (Claim Preparer Disclosure & $1,000 Statutory Penalty): Pursuant to ITA subsections 162(5.1)–(5.3), Part 9 mandates complete disclosure of every external claim preparer who prepared or assisted with the claim, including preparer name, Business Number or SIN, billing structure (contingency percentage, hourly, or flat fee), and total fee (if prepared entirely in-house, Lines 935, 970, and 975 must still be certified). Incomplete, inaccurate, or missing Part 9 information triggers a $1,000 penalty under subsection 162(5.1) to which both the taxpayer and the claim preparer are exposed.

body.text: Under ITA subsections 37(11)–(12) and paragraph 127(9)(m), Form T661 and Schedule 31 / Form T2038(IND) containing prescribed information for each project and expenditure must be filed no later than 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date—which equals 18 months after tax year-end for corporations (6-month T2 due date plus 12 months; for example, June 30, 2027 for a December 31, 2025 year-end) and 17.5 months after year-end for individuals (mid-June of the second following year). The Minister has zero statutory discretion under subsection 220(2.2) to extend this reporting deadline: any project or expenditure omitted as of the 18-month mark is permanently deemed not to be SR&ED.
7.2 CRA Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026)

On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched its optional Pre-Claim Approval program (submitted via My Business Account, with practitioner guidance referencing Form T1322), enabling eligible businesses to obtain upfront technical eligibility confirmation before incurring major project costs. To qualify, a business must operate in Canada as a CCPC, other Canadian corporation, or Canadian partnership, be in good standing with the CRA, and have annual gross business income of less than $25,000,000; each proposed project must not have been claimed previously and must not involve issues under objection or litigation.
The application follows a four-step sequence:

items: Request a Case Number: Complete the brief online request on Canada.ca; existing SR&ED claimants receive a case number in My Business Account within 2 business days, while new SR&ED claimants receive a CRA phone call within 5 business days.

Submit Application in My Business Account: Upload the completed application (covering up to 3 planned projects, anticipated start dates, estimated expenditures, baseline knowledge, technological uncertainties, initial hypotheses, and existing planning documents) before starting work or shortly after commencing.

Meet with a CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA): Within 4 weeks of submission, an assigned RTA conducts a 2-to-5-hour technical meeting (virtual or facility tour) with the claimant's in-house technical lead—mandatory for new SR&ED claimants and discretionary for existing claimants in good standing.

Receive Written Determination & Fast-Track Post-Filing Review: Within 8 weeks of submitting a complete application, the RTA issues a written determination valid for up to 3 years (material project scope changes require notifying the RTA or re-applying; non-approval does not prevent filing a regular SR&ED claim later). Claimants must still file Form T661 and Schedule 31 after year-end, but for refundable claims where every claimed project holds valid Pre-Claim Approval without unapproved material changes, the CRA's expenditure review service standard is cut in half from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days (alongside the 60-day standard for claims accepted as filed).

body.text: 8. Jurisprudence, CRA Review Procedures, and Tax Court Litigation
8.1 Landmark Appellate and Tax Court Precedents

Because subsection 248(1) sets out high-level principles rather than prescriptive industry checklists, Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) decisions govern every SR&ED eligibility dispute.

cells: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 D.T.C. 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520
Tax Court of Canada (May 1998, Bowman J.)

Established the foundational Five-Question Test: (1) technological risk/uncertainty not removable by routine engineering; (2) specific hypotheses aimed at reducing the uncertainty; (3) adherence to the total discipline of the scientific method; (4) technological advancement; and (5) contemporaneous records of hypotheses and test results.
RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, (1998) 99 D.T.C. 5087, 235 N.R. 258
Endorsed Northwest Hydraulic at the appellate level; required objective documentary proof of systematic testing and repeatability.
Summarized and cemented the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria as the governing legal framework under ITA s. 248(1).
Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 FCA 355 & R&D Pro-innovation Inc. v. Canada, 2016 FCA 152
Reaffirmed Northwest Hydraulic, confirming that trial-and-error shop adjustments lacking structured hypothesis testing fail s. 248(1).

Taxpayer rulings confirming manufacturing/analytical projects qualify where parameters lie outside standard operating ranges and systematic experimentation yields new protocols (mapping questions 1 & 4 to "Why" and 2, 3 & 5 to "How").
Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, Docket 2015-125(IT)I
Dismissed claims where only a non-engineer company owner and an external tax consultant testified, actual designers were not called, test parameters went unrecorded, and work was routine.
Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2021 FCA 88 (followed in National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72, Rennie J.A.)

Rejected taxpayer arguments that "scientific method" does not appear in the literal text of s. 248(1); reaffirmed Criterion 3 of Northwest Hydraulic as binding law (followed again by the FCA in May 2022 in denying a consulting firm's appeal).
Logix Data Products Inc. (2021), Dave's Diesel Inc. (2022), JEC Distributors Inc. (2022) & Paveit Construction Inc. (Sept 2025)

Established that technological uncertainty is strictly an objective test, not subjective to non-specialist employees; failure to establish objective industry baselines (including leading no expert evidence on routine vs. system uncertainty in Paveit, Sept 2025) is fatal.

body.text: 8.2 CRA Audit Defence, Administrative Escalation, and Formal Appeals

According to CRA program data for April 1, 2025 to March 31, 2026 cited in Canadian CPA analyses, 24,160 SR&ED claims were filed ($4.6 billion in credits allowed) and 23,677 were processed: 90% were accepted as filed, 6% were accepted with adjustments, 4% were denied, and 92.5% of refundable claims selected for review or service were completed within the 180-day standard. While first-time claimants may receive an educational advisory meeting, claims selected via CORTAX risk scoring or random sampling undergo a formal Technical, Financial, or Coordinated Review—and once selected for review, an SR&ED claim cannot be withdrawn. Defending an SR&ED review or denial follows four strict procedural stages:

items: Review Meeting & Information Requests (30-Day Standard): The RTA and FR initiate contact by phone and follow up with a written agenda and document request (typically granting 30 days to respond; claimant extensions pause the CRA's 180-day processing clock). Direct technical personnel—not third-party consultants—should lead the virtual or on-site walkthrough, presenting contemporaneous source-control commits, test logs, failed prototypes, equipment logs, T4 payroll reconciliations, and trial-balance mappings.

Proposal Letter Written Representations (30-Day Window): Where the RTA or FR proposes partial or full disallowance (or penalties), the CRA issues a draft technical/financial review report and Proposal Letter, providing 30 days to submit targeted written rebuttals and documentary evidence before reassessment.

Three-Step Administrative Dispute Resolution (Application Policy SR&ED 2000-02R): Prior to reassessment, unresolved disagreements may be escalated sequentially: first to the RTA/FR; second to the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) or Financial Review Manager (FRM); and third via a formal Administrative Second Review examining procedural fairness and policy compliance. Crucial Procedural Trap: Requesting an Administrative Second Review does not pause or extend the statutory 90-day Notice of Objection clock once a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued.

Formal Notice of Objection (ITA s. 165) & Tax Court of Canada Appeal (ITA s. 169): Under current enacted law, a Notice of Objection (filed online via My Business Account or by mail on Form T400A to the Chief of Appeals) must be filed within 90 days from the date on the Notice of Assessment or Reassessment (with extensions available only upon application within one year after the 90-day deadline expires). Because CRA Appeals Division reviews frequently take 12 to 24 months, a claimant whose Notice of Objection remains undecided after 90 days may bypass Appeals and file a Notice of Appeal directly with the Tax Court of Canada—electing either the Informal Procedure (where federal tax and penalties in dispute per taxation year do not exceed $25,000, or the appellant elects to cap relief at $25,000) or the General Procedure (unlimited dollar amounts, formal discovery, and independent expert engineering witnesses, with appeal rights to the Federal Court of Appeal).
